note: TWM feeds discrete image latents, actions and rewards through a sequence model, then trains a policy on imagined trajectories. Atari 100k aggregate intervals and a three-game replay ablation address interaction efficiency, not hardware control.

MC-JEPA shares an encoder between image-view agreement and unsupervised optical flow. Flow and dense visual tasks test transferable motion/content features; there is no action-conditioned planner in these experiments.

C-SWM factorizes an image into object slots, predicts their interactions with a graph network and ranks candidate future states. Retrieval performance is not a control return; the deterministic Markov assumption breaks under unobserved randomness.
locator: Fig. 1; §§4.2, 4.7; tkipf/c-swm: eval.py lines 114–149 (pairwise ranking and reciprocal ranks).

note: R2I uses a recurrent state-space sequence model to carry information into imagined actor–critic training. Delaying a cue or reward in controlled memory tasks tests retention; training batch length and imagination horizon are still finite.

UniZero separates the encoded observation from the accessible history used by its transformer and searches the resulting model with MCTS. VisualMatch tests whether an earlier cue can inform a later choice; that is different from pixel forecasting or testing on a robot.

Puppeteer freezes a motion-capture-trained tracker, letting a higher-level planner choose reference motions rather than joint actions. Its simulated visual locomotion tasks and human judgments of movement do not establish dexterous manipulation.

SOLD predicts action-conditioned histories of visual object slots and learns behavior using those dynamics. Three-seed comparisons show a clearer advantage on tasks that require distinguishing relations than on simple reaching; no comparable claim follows for arbitrary clutter.
locator: Fig. 2(a); §§3.1–3.2; §4.2, Table 1 and Fig. 4 (Specific versus Distinct).

note: Dream to Fly compares DreamerV3 against model-free racing agents on three tracks. The Figure-8 transfer experiment closes the loop through a physical quadrotor but supplies Habitat-rendered images, not an onboard camera feed.

A strong model-free Craftax agent supplies the baseline for adding Dyna with warmup, a patch nearest-neighbor tokenizer and block teacher forcing. The incremental comparison matters: gains over older agents cannot all be credited to imagination, and a tiled game favors patch tokenization.

BMPC trains its proposal policy to imitate improved MPC actions and refreshes targets by reanalysis. DMControl curves separate the network acting alone from the planner; gains are particularly relevant when the planner is stronger than its proposal, not uniformly across tasks.
locator: Figs. 1–2; §§4.1–4.2, 5.1 (28 DMControl tasks; ten shown in Fig. 3).

note: DINO-world predicts frozen DINOv2 patch features at queried locations and times. Segmentation/depth probes applied to forecast features, plausibility from surprise, and action-conditioned planning after adaptation are three separate tests; this is not DINO-WM.

ScaleZero studies interference in a shared UniZero-style planner, routing updates through experts and varying capacity during training. The reported interaction saving for dynamic scaling is measured against a matched performance target on DMC18, not a universal speedup.

A goal-conditioned value learned with an IQL-style objective gives JEPA planning a cost beyond raw feature distance. Success is measured on start–goal pairs in Wall and Maze with MPPI; sparse coverage of distant pairs makes long-range values less dependable.

JEPA-VLA probes frozen visual features for task-relevant state and fuses V-JEPA 2 features into an action model. LIBERO, LIBERO-plus and real-task comparisons assess the resulting policy, not a new action-conditioned simulator.

H-WM searches logical transitions and supplies visual subgoals to a faster VLA. On LIBERO-LoHo, progress and completion diverge when a policy skips a subtask. The hierarchy here is symbolic plus visual, not the multirate latent MPC of HWM.

LPWM uses per-particle latent actions to sample different object futures. Video quality on stochastic sequences and success after using the representation for imitation on PandaPush/OGBench test different capabilities; strong rollouts do not guarantee success on long compositions.

Variational JEPA predicts a distribution over target latents. Its control sufficiency theorem assumes the representation already preserves predictive and cost information. In the linear distractor experiment deterministic JEPA is more stable at the highest noise setting. Not the V-JEPA video model.
locator: PMLR v306, Download PDF: §3.1 p. 3; Theorem 5.2 p. 6; Fig. 3 p. 8 and Fig. 5 p. 9.

note: Temporal-Distance JEPA learns a directed distance from trajectory gaps. With episodes, model and search budget held fixed, the learned cost can help navigation yet hurt Push-T after contact. Better correlation with elapsed steps need not mean better action selection.

V-JEPA-LM trains a language readout using paired video transformations whose answers must change. Its clip-level multiple-choice tests assess sensitivity to motion and ordering; they neither require robot actions nor test hour-long memory.
locator: Fig. 2; §§4, 5.1–5.2; evaluation protocol in App. C; kkt94/Llama-V-JEPA-LM: llama_vjepa_lm/modeling_jepa_llm.py (SpectralBridge), README §8.

note: MAD (Mapping-Aware Dreamer) reconstructs occupancy and visibility in a robot-centered grid from depth and proprioception. The indoor flight study tests its learned representation; at deployment the policy does not use the decoded map for explicit feasibility checks. Distinct from ScanDreamer.
locator: Figs. 1–2; §§III-B, IV, V; direct paper behind the bare identifier 2606.04534.

note: DriveDreamer-2 maps a user scenario to agent trajectories, generates road structure and conditions a multiview video generator. nuScenes quality results vary with the supplied views and frames; FVD is not driving-policy success. A sequel, not another citation for DriveDreamer.

ADriver-I infers speed/steering from visual and action history and conditions a diffusion model on the inferred controls to generate four frames. The authors report control error and video metrics separately; the private highway data have lower control variance than nuScenes.

OccSora compresses sequences of semantic occupancy volumes, then denoises scene tokens given an ego trajectory. Reconstruction and generation evaluate voxel scenes, not camera realism. Voxel resolution and inconsistent moving-object detail limit interpretation.
locator: Fig. 2; §§4.2–4.3, 5; wzzheng/OccSora: step02.py lines 223–244 (ground truth and token export).

note: DrivingWorld autoregresses over front-view image and vehicle-pose tokens. The nuScenes comparisons and long-rollout demonstrations test visual generation and control following; a scripted yaw sweep does not test traffic reactivity.

GEM conditions a denoiser on ego trajectory, object features and human pose to generate egocentric images and depth. Human raters compare short and longer unconditional clips; this complements FVD but does not validate counterfactual physical outcomes.
locator: Fig. 2; §§3.2–3.4, 5.3–5.4; §5.3 compares 2.5 s and 15 s clips.

note: World Engine mines rare logged driving events, reconstructs scenes and simulates other agents for policy post-training. Rare-log replay improves open-loop scores without the same gain in interactive evaluation. Event mining cannot retrieve a failure type absent from the logs.

SimVTA renders a matched future for selected candidate trajectories rather than supervising every candidate with the logged video. NAVSIM v1 rises from 86.2 to 91.3 PDMS; HUGSIM is a separate closed-loop test. High prediction error can also reveal a bad render.
locator: OpenDriveLab project page → arXiv 2610.13781; Figs. 1–2; §§3.2–3.4, 4.2; App. G. Code: OpenDriveLab/SimVTA README, Matched Futures for Alternative Actions.

note: RoboDreamer factors instructions and combines conditional diffusion components to generate visual plans. Human judgments of novel instruction combinations and execution in RLBench are separate evaluations. Single-view generation limits spatial disambiguation.

FLARE adds alignment with a future embedding to a flow-matching action policy. It compares against a policy-only model trained for extra steps and tests transfer on RoboCasa and a small GR-1 suite. An aligned hidden state is not a decoded future frame.

DreamVLA splits forecast queries into moving regions, depth and semantics for action prediction. Motion supervision selects relevant pixels rather than reconstructing a whole frame. The benchmark code and checkpoint card document target preparation and CALVIN evaluation, not a calibrated simulator.
locator: Figs. 2–4; §3.3; Zhangwenyao1/DreamVLA: data_process/cotrack_extractor.py; WenyaoZhang/DreamVLA model card, Data Processing.

note: Motus combines video and action generation at different temporal rates and uses latent actions to include unlabeled data. RoboTwin randomized success is distinct from the real-arm partial-credit metric, where accomplishing intermediate goals earns credit.

mimic-video conditions an action decoder on internal video-model representations. An oracle experiment swaps predicted futures for expert-video latents; the gap isolates forecasting difficulty but the oracle is unavailable at deployment. Actual policies are evaluated on SIMPLER-Bridge and LIBERO.
locator: §III (oracle study, figure comparing expert and predicted video); §§IV-C–D, V-A; Tables I–II.

note: SANA-WM uses hybrid attention, camera-pose conditioning and a refiner for minute-scale video. Trajectory error and visual scores concern camera motion, not a robot's manipulation actions. The authors note drift and the lack of explicit persistent 3D memory.

WristWorld estimates wrist projections from anchor views, then conditions video synthesis on geometry and appearance. Dropping the projection harms fidelity; the output is an additional observation of a trajectory, not evidence that the model predicts effects of new actions.

World4RL fits separate diffusion dynamics and a task-success classifier before refining an imitation policy in frozen imagined dynamics. The six-task Meta-World success comparison is downstream of, and not interchangeable with, the video-quality results.

SRPO uses successful and unsuccessful policy rollouts as references in a frozen video representation to shape progress rewards. LIBERO and perturbation tests concern the resulting policy; the encoder does not generate an environment. siiRL is the host framework.

NORA-1.5 ranks proposed actions by predicted distance to a goal in V-JEPA-2-AC or by agreement with recorded actions, then trains from preferences. SimplerEnv policy scores do not turn either proxy into ground-truth task reward.
locator: Fig. 1; §3.2 (reward designs and preference construction); Table 1; declare-lab/nora-1.5: training/post_training/label_generated_data.py (goal-latent L1).

note: VLA-Reasoner performs test-time tree search around a pretrained policy, using sampled candidate actions and a visual value estimator. Comparing the same backbone with and without search on simulated and physical tasks tests the added computation, not a better base policy trained from scratch.

MoWM trains pixel and feature predictors separately, freezes them, and trains an action denoiser on their modulated features. CALVIN measures completed instruction chains. The linked default-branch README contains only the project name; it does not substantiate reproducibility.

FlowVLA interleaves optical-motion and appearance tokens during autoregressive pretraining, then adapts to actions. LIBERO and SimplerEnv evaluate policies; qualitative Bridge V2 predictions serve a different purpose. Here flow means visual motion, not a flow-matching control head.

UD-VLA denoises discrete image and action blocks with directed information flow between them and bidirectional attention inside each block. The paper compares joint, independent and autoregressive decoding on CALVIN; average chain length is not single-task success.
locator: §§3.1–3.3, Fig. 1; §§4.2–4.3, Tables 2 and 7; note CALVIN ABCD → D protocol.

note: dVLA uses a discrete diffusion backbone for subgoal images, reasoning text and actions. LIBERO suite results and ten trials per physical task are different evidence; a visual warning in a failure example is not a verified safety mechanism.

WorldEval injects Policy2Vec representations into a video model and scores generated manipulation outcomes with a verifier. Paired physical tests check policy ordering across four policies. High rank agreement need not mean calibrated success probabilities for new policies. Not WorldGym.
locator: Fig. 2; §§3.2–3.3, 4.1–4.2; Fig. 4 and Table 2 (Pearson correlation and rank violations).

note: MMaDA-VLA denoises masked goal observations and action chunks in parallel. A physical-arm comparison includes pick/place, drawers and stacking; the reported grasp and stacking failures illustrate why a plausible goal image is insufficient for precise contact.

RDT2 trains on handheld UMI demonstrations and vision–language data, then distills a multistep action expert for faster inference. The no-finetuning test used new objects, instructions and embodiments in controlled, constant-light laboratory scenes; this is a narrower claim than arbitrary household transfer.

MolmoAct2 combines an embodied-reasoning backbone with an action expert conditioned on per-layer keys and values. A controlled LIBERO-Long ablation first tests the backbone using only discrete actions; the gain there cannot be attributed to continuous flow decoding.
locator: Fig. 1; §§2.2, 4; §6.7, Tables 10 and 12–13 (backbone, flow samples and tuning).

note: Galaxea G0.5 generates optional reasoning tokens and compact action codes in one autoregressive stream. Embodiment-aware grouping omits inactive parts. DROID and referring-context tests distinguish instruction grounding from motor execution; occlusion can still defeat the name-only prompt.

Hy-Embodied-0.5-VLA combines temporal visual memory and a flow action expert with FlowPRO offline preference learning. RoboTwin averages 100 stochastic trials per task across 50 tasks, split into clean and randomized scenes; several comparison scores are taken from the other teams' reports.

Being-H0.7 aligns a train-time branch that can see the future with a branch restricted to current context, so the latter can act without a future video. The paper's standard LIBERO and perturbed LIBERO-plus results differ substantially; its real-world suites also have overlapping task tags.

AffordanceVLA predicts what to interact with, where, and how, then conditions action generation on those intermediates. LIBERO suite averages hide a weaker long-horizon score; CALVIN evaluates how many successive commands are completed instead.

Three distinct Astra studies share this row. One varies training-set context and interaction budget; another reports 24/50 RoboDojo successes for hybrid π0.5 control versus 13/50 direct; the GPT-GEAR study reports 4/36 zero-shot on LIBERO-GeoMotion. None is a single all-benchmark model score.

AgiBot's dated GO-3 Preview announcement describes WRAM selecting future representations for action training, followed by hybrid post-training. The three leaderboard firsts are claims by the developer, not independently measured here. This source is a release article, not a paper or shipped implementation.
locator: First-party newsroom release, 29 Oct 2026: opening benchmark graphic (RoboDojo/RoboTwin/RoboColiseum); Pre-Training Scaling section (CoAE, SVP, KASO).

note: LingBot-VLA 2.0 has a July report and a first-party 6B model card. The 60k-hour mixture includes 10k human-video hours, not 60k hours of robot trajectories. A sparse action expert and present/future teacher queries are evaluated with separate progress and completion scores on GM-100 tasks.
locator: Fig. 1; §§3.1, 4.1–4.2, 5.2; HF robbyant/lingbot-vla-v2-6b and robbyant/lingbot-vla-v2 README, Dual-Query Distillation.

note: TwinRL expands a demonstration workspace in a digital twin, warms up RL there and transfers rollouts into real-robot replay. Four real tasks track in- and out-of-distribution workspace regions across training. The method still learns online on hardware; it is not pure sim-to-real transfer.
locator: Fig. 3; §§III-C–E, IV-B–C; Fig. 5 and Tables I–II. The v4 title says TwinRL.

note: FIND chooses a feasible task from the current workspace, evaluates before/after images, and gates residual corrections to a frozen policy with a critic. In one six-hour, 456-episode run, 426 episodes needed no manual scene recovery; that is an autonomy measure, not 426 task successes.
locator: Figs. 1–2; §§III-B, IV-B, Table II (manual recovery) and Fig. 3 (ablations).

note: The Wuji-hand study reuses a learned hand-command codec for imitation, operator corrections and residual RL. All five tasks succeeded in 20/20 final trials each, but all involve the same marker. The latent-versus-joint residual comparison is more diagnostic than a claim of universal dexterity.

TacClaw-Infinity uses touch onset/release to segment demonstrations and to anchor manipulated objects across views. Table II measures reachability, whereas Table IV tests actual manipulation on three robots. The release roadmap distinguishes replay tools from forthcoming policy training/evaluation code.
locator: Fig. 2; §§III-C, V-B, V-D; Tables II/IV; tacclaw-infinity/TacClaw-Infinity README, News and Robot Replay and Evaluation.

note: Open-AoE turns distributed smartphone recordings into segmented, labeled manipulation data. The updated vocabulary and temporal coverage audit is on 100 hours, not the entire roughly 2,000-hour release. Usable history–future windows measure data continuity rather than robot success.

EgoVerse standardizes video, hand keypoints and camera poses across capture rigs. EgoVerse-A repeats flagship tasks under a shared protocol; EgoVerse-I emphasizes breadth. Robot co-training gains should be compared within settings because demonstration speeds and reset ranges differ.

UMI-FT calibrates fingertip force/torque measurements and separates slow learned targets from faster feedback control. Skewering and contact modulation ablations distinguish force regulation from predicting gripper width or detecting contact alone. Success counts refer to these specific tools and contacts.

UMI-on-Air guides diffusion samples with the tracking cost of the intended embodiment. Transfer to a physical aerial manipulator is tested on three tasks; peg insertion was five trials with motion capture providing vehicle state. Embodiment-agnostic demonstrations do not imply a controller-free deployment.

GR-RL filters demonstrations with a progress critic, augments them by symmetry, then steers an action generator using online experience. The staged comparison on ByteMini-v2 shoe lacing separates filtering gains from later RL gains; it establishes a specialist, not broad generalization.

WMPO alternates a VLA and video dynamics to generate on-policy experience in imagination. Training the world model only on expert successes misses the policy's failures; the physical insertion study uses 200 expert demonstrations and 128 additional policy trajectories before imagined updates.
locator: Fig. 2; §3.2 (Policy Behavior Alignment); §§4.1, 4.6 (MimicGen versus physical insertion).

note: PLD trains task-specific residual specialists, lets them take over part-way through a generalist rollout to generate recovery data, then refits the generalist by supervision. LIBERO task coverage in Fig. 2 counts distinct tasks, not demonstrations; specialist RL is not required at deployment.
locator: Figs. 2–3; §§3.1–3.2, 4.1–4.3 (LIBERO and a custom SimplerEnv suite).

note: DSRL learns which noise to pass into a frozen diffusion policy, rather than adding a motor residual after decoding. Noise aliasing lets multiple noise inputs share action-space experience; offline and online tests improve on imitation, but steering is limited by behaviors the base model can produce.

DemoGen edits point-cloud observations and action trajectories to move a demonstration to new object arrangements. Workspace success maps test spatial coverage. At equal demonstration count, single-view synthetic point clouds do not fully replace real demonstrations because visibility changes with pose.
locator: Fig. 2; §§III-A, IV, V-B; Fig. 8 (synthetic versus real view mismatch).

note: Policy Decorator learns an online action residual around a fixed base policy and controls exploration. ManiSkill/Adroit experiments test correction without full-model finetuning. Keeping the backbone frozen avoids updating it, not paying its inference cost at every rollout.

FlowPolicy uses point clouds and robot state to condition an action flow with a consistency objective. Reported inference time versus DP3 is 19.9 versus 145.7 ms in the authors' setup; the success comparison covers 37 Adroit/Meta-World tasks, not a sevenfold success improvement.
locator: Figs. 1–2; Method → Consistency Flow Matching; Experiments → Tables 1 (latency) and 2 (success).

note: The human-activity pretraining pipeline reconstructs metric hand/camera motion, segments atomic actions and adds instructions. Predicting a human hand trajectory zero-shot and controlling a physical robot after finetuning are different transfer claims; imperfect reconstruction propagates into the labels.
locator: Fig. 2; §§3.1–3.4, 4.1; §§5–6 (video diversity, transfer and reconstruction limits).

note: DLR discovers behavior modes in demonstrations, clones a mode-conditioned policy and refines each with sparse task reward. The generated trajectories pretrain VLAs on LIBERO-90 before downstream finetuning. The test is transfer from diverse simulator trajectories, not new skill discovery in an uninstrumented home.
locator: Fig. 1; §§4.3–4.5 (decoupling diversity and reward), 5.1 (pretraining and downstream suites).
